_comment: The compatibility matrix, checked in. One source of truth for which of the three playback
tiers a given file gets on a given browser.
Every row is (what the file is) x (what the browser reported) -> (the route). Changing an
answer here changes what a real person gets for a real file, so it changes in a diff that
somebody has to read, rather than inside a function nobody re-reads after it works once.
`why` is not decoration. A row whose reason nobody can state is a row nobody understands, and
the next person to touch this file needs to know which rows are load-bearing.
All rows are 1920x1080 at 30fps on 4 cores unless they say otherwise, which is comfortably
above realtime, so these rows test the routing decision and not the realtime gate. The gate
has its own tests in test_policy.py, where the resolutions are the interesting variable.

The remux tier is currently unreachable: policy.decide falls through to transcode where it would have remuxed. These rows keep the codec/container shapes that identify the tier so that re-enabling it is a matter of flipping the expected route back, with the cases already written.

cases.why: The universal case. H.264/AAC in MP4 on any browser: served off disk, no ffmpeg.
A capable browser does not make the simple case any harder.

AV1 direct-play. The most valuable row in the file: AV1 is the most expensive codec to transcode and the most widely supported to decode, so it must never take the expensive path when the browser can read it.
HEVC in MP4 on Chrome 107+ or Safari, where a hardware decoder exists. Assuming otherwise is years out of date.
WebM is native to Chrome and Firefox and needs nothing done to it.

A REMUX CASE, converted per segment on this viewing. A stream copy cannot cut at an arbitrary point (input seeking lands on the preceding keyframe), so on real media with multi-second GOPs copied segments overlap and do not match the durations the playlist declares; the copy is a whole-file repackage instead (see policy.decide). As a remux: the tier-2 case that must not be skipped. The browser decodes HEVC fine; it cannot demux Matroska. A stream copy fixes the container for near-zero cost with no quality loss at all: transcoding this would be a full re-encode to solve a packaging problem.

A REMUX CASE, converted per segment on this viewing. A stream copy cannot cut at an arbitrary point (input seeking lands on the preceding keyframe), so on real media with multi-second GOPs copied segments overlap and do not match the durations the playlist declares; the copy is a whole-file repackage instead (see policy.decide). As a remux: H.264 in Matroska, which is a common shape for downloaded content. Same reasoning: repackage, do not re-encode.

A REMUX CASE, converted per segment on this viewing. A stream copy cannot cut at an arbitrary point (input seeking lands on the preceding keyframe), so on real media with multi-second GOPs copied segments overlap and do not match the durations the playlist declares; the copy is a whole-file repackage instead (see policy.decide). As a remux: AV1 in Matroska. This row is why segments are fragmented MP4 rather than MPEG-TS: TS cannot carry AV1, so a TS pipeline would force this file to transcode, the single most expensive thing the machine can do, for a container swap.
A browser with no HEVC decoder. Genuinely undecodable, so it is genuinely re-encoded.
The worst case identified: an older iPhone against an AV1 library. Expensive and unavoidable: the client genuinely cannot decode it.
Video is fine, audio is not. Sound counts: a file whose audio will not play is not playable.
An exotic legacy codec no browser has ever decoded. The fallback still has to exist, and this is what it is for.
A silent clip. A NULL audio codec is the absence of audio, not an unsupported codec: reading it as one would transcode every silent file in the library for nothing.
